articles.title: NAZA: Why are old Gaza allegations causing new fury in Israel?
articles.summary: Israeli soldiers’ Gaza testimony causes backlash across much of the country’s political establishment.
articles.body:
Israel’s bitter political divisions are particularly sharp before the country’s October elections. But the furious response to a new documentary about the military’s actions in the genocidal war on Gaza has revealed an issue that much of Israel’s political and media establishment appears united on.

Few of the central allegations in NAZA, made by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, are new. Reports that the Israeli military was relying on artificial intelligence systems to generate targets in Gaza, often killing the inhabitants of entire buildings to kill just one individual identified by the system, were reported in April 2024.

Other accusations against Israel, such as committing genocide, deliberately causing a famine, and unlawfully killing children, have also not received much attention in Israel.

In contrast, NAZA has unleashed a litany of abuse from across Israel, and brought the allegations to the centre of Israel’s political debate.

Culture Minister Miki Zohar reacted to the film’s premiere at the Venice Film Festival – where it received a 25-minute standing ovation – by calling for the directors to be stripped of their citizenship and to be investigated by the internal intelligence service for treason.

Army chief Eyal Zamir has dismissed the film as being built on blood libel and ordered a legal probe to hunt down its military and intelligence sources.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also cited the film when advancing legislation to revoke citizenship from anyone deemed to be smearing the country’s soldiers, while in the coastal city of Ashdod, graffiti branding the directors “traitors” has appeared on the walls.

“You can’t really understand the extent of the madness from outside of the country,” Orly Noy, an editor at Local Call, which first carried many of the accusations contained in the film, said. “They’re attacking the friends and families of [the filmmakers] Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. They’re talking about revoking their citizenship. They’re asking the Shin Bet to investigate them – for making a film, and it isn’t just the politicians. Journalists, who you might expect to show some kind of solidarity with them, are competing to attack them. It’s scary.”

In late 2025, the Committee to Protect Journalists reported escalating censorship and harassment in Israel, with Israeli journalists telling the organisation that the media’s approach had become “part of the war effort” and, by extension, significantly shaped Israeli view of their war on Gaza.

In October 2025, a study by the Israeli think tank Molad found that only 3 percent of Channel 12’s coverage of the first six months of the war mentioned Gaza’s humanitarian crisis. Of 206 war-related images and video clips broadcast by the network, Israel’s most-watched channel, only two showed Palestinian civilian casualties.

Nevertheless, before the film’s release, polls found that most Israelis believed the coverage they were receiving of the military’s conduct in Gaza was balanced.

“I guess it was because the mainstream media outlets in Israel did not investigate the conduct of the army during the war in Gaza, and hardly covered the war from the Palestinian point of view,” Anat Saragusti, the Israeli jurist and journalist responsible for press freedom at the Union of Journalists in Israel, said of the shock that had accompanied the release of the film. “[The Israeli media] hardly reported on the human toll and the scale of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.”

Compounding the gap, Saragusti said, was a deep-seated national narrative: that the war had been imposed on Israel, that Hamas had carried out a massacre on October 7, 2023, and that Hamas’s use of civilians as human shields made mass casualties in Gaza all but unavoidable.

Palestinian deaths, in this telling, were framed less as the product of Israeli conduct than as collateral damage forced on Israel by its enemy’s tactics, she said.

“Even journalists that usually support the anti-Netanyahu bloc have criticised the filmmakers,” Israeli political sociologist Daniel Bar-Tal said.

“Israeli Jews deny the genocide,” he continued, “Even all the opposition parties joined the vicious criticism of the filmmakers.”

The language used against the filmmakers has been echoed by some of Netanyahu’s most prominent political rivals.

On Monday, former military chief and one of Netanyahu’s principal rivals Gadi Eisenkot denounced the film for “moral blindness, a detachment from reality, and harm to the State of Israel in a difficult hour”.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who is also running in October’s election, called the film a “horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters”.

“Everything gets heightened the closer to the election we get,” Noy said. “But I think only now, for those of us who live here, is the extent of the fascism becoming clear. Journalists, politicians and the media are forming some kind of incitement machine.”

“I’ve had anxieties over where Israel had been going for a long time,” she said, “but right now I’m genuinely worried for my friends and colleagues.”

articles.title: Why rock band Queen practised early harmonies in a Cornish cave
articles.summary: Drummer Roger Taylor says Queen perfected their singing in a cave on a beach in Cornwall.
articles.body:
Queen drummer Roger Taylor has recalled how his mum organised the band's first ever concert to raise funds for the British Red Cross.

The show in Truro in June 1970 featured Taylor on drums, Brian May on guitar and vocals by Freddie Mercury, then known as Fred Bulsara.

Taylor also revealed how the group perfected their trademark harmonies by singing in a cave on a Cornish beach because they loved the "big sound".

The musician was speaking ahead of the release of his latest solo album, Violence Insane in a Beautiful World.

The Truro gig was Mercury's first live performance with Taylor and May and he used the occasion to announce their new name, Queen.

The set consisted of songs they had written themselves, including Stone Cold Crazy and Son and Daughter, as well as rock 'n' roll covers.

Queen went on to become one of the most successful rock bands in history, selling more than 300 million records worldwide.

They also gained a reputation as a formidable live act, filling stadiums around the world.

Taylor was born in King's Lynn, Norfolk, and was drawn to drumming from an early age.

"I got all my mother's saucepans and turned them upside down. She had some big wooden knitting needles, which I used to use to sort of play them. And I would pretend I was playing the drums, but I was playing the saucepans."

Taylor moved to Cornwall with his family when he was seven. He sang in the Truro Cathedral Choir for about a year and played drums with various local bands as a teenager.

"We lived by the sea at first, but just a few months. Then we moved to Truro which, of course, is in the middle [of Cornwall] and is kind of the capital really. It was a nice place to grow up. Cornwall's beautiful, you know."

At the age of 18, Roger Taylor headed to London to study dentistry, later switching to biology. But his heart was set on music.

He answered an advert on a college noticeboard for a drummer to join a band called Smile that included Brian May.

Smile broke up in the spring of 1970 but the group still had a booking to fulfill at Truro City Hall, now known as the Hall for Cornwall.

With Freddie Mercury on board, Smile became Queen and the Truro gig marked their live debut.

"I think we were paid £50, which was an enormous amount in those days.

"We had just started Queen then and Freddie hadn't really developed his voice, his vocal capacities, to the full.

"He sounded quite alarming some of the time. He sounded a little bit like a strangled sheep at times with a very fast falsetto. But of course he kind of invented himself out of it all.

"We didn't realise at the time what a great musician he was. A great piano player. A fantastic songwriter. We didn't know what a gem we had at first."

Taylor admitted his mum was "rather alarmed" by their performance but she admired Freddie's courtesy and style.

"She could never believe how Freddie had such beautiful manners and he was always so deferential and polite and how his trousers were always immaculately creased," he said.

"We found out he was putting his trousers under the mattress and pressing them as he slept."

Taylor said calling the group Queen was Freddie's idea.

"We were discussing daft names. One was Build Your Own Boat, which is a sort of prog name, I suppose.

"There were various things, you know. But it [Queen] was a good name. It was simple. It was easy to remember and direct."

Taylor recalled practising harmonies with May and Mercury in the caves at Chapel Porth beach in St Agnes.

"I think we must have been in caves because of the nice reverberation, echo in there. So it sounds bigger," he said.

"It would have been a nice place to sing. Bit like singing in a big church or something. The sound rattles around everywhere."

It was an early hint of the powerhouse vocals that became a hallmark of hits like Bohemian Rhapsody and Somebody to Love.

"We had a great blend between the three of us. The three voices had different characteristics. But they went together to make a very good sound when we harmonised."

In the summer of 1971, Queen played a dozen gigs in Cornwall over six weeks, with John Deacon on bass completing their classic line-up.

Many of the shows were organised by Taylor, using his contacts in the county, including dates at Hayle Rugby Club, the Driftwood Spars pub in St Agnes and the band's first open-air concert at the Carnon Downs Festival.

There was also an unlikely appearance at the Royal Navy airbase RNAS Culdrose where the group performed for service personnel in the Warrant Officers and Senior Rates Mess.

Taylor said: "We would play anywhere that would give us a gig."

"We all lived in a nice little cottage in a tiny village called Devereux and I was getting up every morning and working on a farm which was very hard but we were broke, we didn't have any money so it was tough."

Taylor said he still has a house on the Helford River in Cornwall and his son Rufus - who's the drummer for The Darkness - has a pub on the other side of the water.

"I love to get down there. Don't get down enough," he said.

articles.title: Jennifer Aniston’s romance with Jim Curtis faces celebrity relationship trap, expert warns
articles.summary: Matchmaker Gina Hendrix says Jennifer Aniston may be making classic celebrity relationship mistakes with boyfriend Jim Curtis by trying to build him up.
articles.body: Jennifer Aniston’s relationship with hypnotherapist and life coach Jim Curtis has gotten serious in the more than a year and a half since they started dating, but a matchmaker worries the "Friends" star could be making classic mistakes as the higher-profile partner. "I think one of the biggest mistakes is when a woman tries to kind of manage the guy," Los Angeles-based matchmaker Gina Hendrix told Fox News Digital. "When a woman steps into this role, and it's always a great, successful, amazing woman, she thinks, ‘I did it for myself, I can do it for you too,’ and she tries to build the guy up." Hendrix warned that the guy often "ends up with all this new great life, but then he resents her for the help, and she takes on a very unsexy role, and then usually it just all fizzles out from there." JENNIFER ANISTON’S BOYFRIEND, JIM CURTIS, REVEALS WHAT 'FRIENDS' STAR IS REALLY LIKE BEHIND CLOSED DOORS She said it takes an "incredibly secure person" to date a celebrity and "share that kind of spotlight, but still be out of the spotlight to keep this relationship afloat." It’s always better to "keep your relationship out of the public eye as much as humanly possible for so many reasons, and if you can live a life where it's under the radar, and you can live a life that is as private as you could possibly have," she added. THOMAS RHETT REVEALS WHY HE AND WIFE LAUREN REJECT CELEBRITY PERKS FOR COUNTRY LIFE Hendrix said she appreciates it when celebrity spouses avoid red carpet events. "You really should just keep it out, keep it away as far as you can" from the public eye, she added. "I think one of the biggest mistakes is when a woman tries to kind of manage the guy." And I don't know him, don't know her, but it does seem like that is the route you want to take versus, you know, going on social media with your guy and trying to help build him up." JENNIFER ANISTON, BOYFRIEND JIM CURTIS’ CHEMISTRY SHINES AS SHE REVEALS ‘DEEP FEAR’ DURING INTERVIEW Speaking specifically about Aniston’s relationship, Hendrix, who clarified that she doesn't know Aniston or Curtis, said: "For whatever reason, she’s decided to sort of help him with his social media." SYDNEY SWEENEY, SCOOTER BRAUN ROMANCE FACES BIGGEST CHALLENGE YET AS EXPERT WARNS COUPLE TO 'BE PREPARED' Earlier this week, Hendrix posted a video on her Instagram, saying Aniston was making all the "classic, biggest mistakes" in a relationship involving a woman who is more successful than her partner, especially in trying to bring him up to her level. In the past, I’ve felt this idea of, ‘I need you to be in love with me …’ I wasn’t searching for love anymore. And what do I feel now? I feel real joy, real presence, real calmness, real partnership." He said in his own life coaching that 82% of his clients are women, attributing that partially to his "nurturing and empathetic" tone. "It’s softer," he said. He told the reporter that he aims to embody the "divine masculine" and be "a person that is not disrupted easily, so I can hold your fear, trauma, suffering, chaos. Like a tree with deep roots, where in a storm you’ll find safety." He noted that he's "very careful" how he engages as a newly-minted celebrity, which includes not reading anything about his relationship. "It’s certainly not helping me, and it’s sensational," he said. "So I have decided it’s better if I don’t look." articles.title: In Gaza, actors perform a war they are still living
articles.summary: In Gaza, Palestinian actors turn stories of siege and loss into theatre, while confronting the same fears and hardships.
articles.body:
Sheikh Radwan, Gaza – Before Abu Qasai Qaddoura can begin acting, he has to find something to burn.

At six in the morning, the 42-year-old walks to a stall in Sheikh Radwan, where his family has been displaced, to buy firewood. It costs seven shekels ($2) per kilogram. When he cannot afford it, he scavenges for something else to burn – cardboard, plastic or pieces of wood salvaged from destroyed homes.

He lights a small fire so his family can keep warm and cook a meal. He then washes the black soot from his hands before leaving his home for rehearsal.

The journey takes two hours on foot. Qaddoura avoids a main road clogged with rubble and where he says Israeli gunfire poses a danger, taking side streets instead.

By the time he reaches the rehearsal space – a makeshift fabric-and-plastic tent pitched in the car park of Gaza City’s Rashad al-Shawa Cultural Centre, his knees hurt and he struggles to catch his breath.

“I arrive at the rehearsal. I’m exhausted but immediately get to work because we don’t even have time for a short break,” he says.

Weary and quiet, Qaddoura sits slumped as he speaks, his hands resting heavily on his knees. On stage, he plays a doctor trapped inside a Gaza hospital. The baby doll cradled in his arms is his character’s son. There is no anesthetic. He must amputate the child’s leg himself. The baby dies.

The scene is based on the real-life experience of a father in Gaza, whose video the actors have watched.

Until now, Qaddoura had never acted. Before the war, he worked behind the camera as a production manager and sound technician for local media companies. Israeli airstrikes in northern Gaza destroyed his home in al-Tawam.

Now he and his wife, along with their children – Ghazal, 15, Qusai, 12, and Sham, seven – live in a single room on the rooftop of a rented house, sheltered by a plastic tarp.

When he holds the child during rehearsal, the face he sees is not always the character’s son.

“I wasn’t just playing a character; I was staring at my own children’s faces,” Qaddoura says. “Every time I held that child on stage, terror gripped my heart that tomorrow this could be one of my own sons. I couldn’t stop the tears because the fear felt too real.”

On stage, Qaddoura does not break character. He keeps holding the boy until director Ali Abu Yasin calls for them to stop.

Then he collapses into sobs, and the rehearsal stops. For 15 minutes, Qaddoura sits quietly at the side of the stage, sipping water, uncertain whether he can perform it again.

“I remembered my own children, and how a father could stand helpless and broken before his child’s wound,” he says afterward.

Eventually Ali Abu Yasin, the play’s director, calls the actors back. Qaddoura gets on his feet, takes his place and does it all again.

This is what Abu Yasin has asked his actors to do: take experiences they are already struggling to survive and turn them into theatre.

Abu Yasin speaks calmly and deliberately, even amid the chaos surrounding the production. He has spent 37 years as an actor, playwright and director, training generations of performers in Gaza. His productions have travelled beyond the enclave to countries including Egypt and Tunisia, where he won a best actor award at the Tunis International Theatre Festival.

But the theatrical landscape he built his career on has been steadily disappearing. Al-Mishal Cultural Centre was destroyed in an Israeli airstrike in 2018. The Rashad al-Shawa Cultural Centre in Gaza City was damaged in Israeli attacks in 2023. By March 2026, UNESCO had verified damage to 164 cultural sites in Gaza since October 7, 2023, including 128 buildings of historical or artistic interest.

For Abu Yasin, the problem was now immediate: Where do you produce theatre when you no longer have a theatre?

His play 50 Minutes in Gaza began in April 2026 as a theatrical writing workshop supported by the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation. Fourteen young men and women were supposed to participate. As the war continued, some were wounded and left Gaza for treatment; others were displaced or unable to make the journey.

Eight eventually made it into the production.

They had originally joined to learn the craft of writing for the stage. But once the script was finished, the participants decided to perform it themselves.

The foundation covered basic production costs and gave the performers a small honorarium for their work, rather than a salary. Qaddoura says his family otherwise survives largely on humanitarian aid. Abu Yasin insists money wasn’t what kept the actors making dangerous, exhausting journeys to rehearsals.

Instead, he says, the work became a form of psychological and emotional release: a way for the actors to process what they were living through and ultimately, to offer a similar outlet to audiences enduring the war around them.

“We are ordinary humans, running after clean water, electricity, food trucks and a livelihood so we can survive amidst skyrocketing prices,” Abu Yasin says.

“But when we step onto the theatre stage, we feel more alive.”

The actors squeezed into fabric tents pitched directly on hot asphalt in the car park of the Rashad al-Shawa Cultural Centre, where the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate had established its tent and site.

Displaced families lived on the other side of the canvas. The air smelled of sweat, dust and burning plastic. Arguments and traffic drifted inside. Above them was the persistent buzz of Israeli reconnaissance drones.

After 12 days, amid gunfire in the area, the company moved again.

This time they rehearsed inside a small partitioned room in Ajwa cafe, a partially damaged building in central Gaza City.

There was no ventilation. Electricity was unreliable. Music was played from a mobile phone.

And there was almost nothing from which to build a set.

With timber scarce and increasingly valuable as firewood, the actors gathered pieces of wood and damaged tent canvas. With the help of a displaced craftsman, they built the set themselves.

“When you ask me about difficulties, it seems the better question is: What was available or normal?” Abu Yasin says.

“The difficulty was in everything; the work literally emerged from under the rubble, its set came from tents, and the actors were still dusting gunpowder off their bodies.”

Some actors, like Qaddoura, walked for hours through destroyed streets to reach him, arriving with rubble dust on their clothes.

Then they began pretending to be people trapped by war.

One day in May, actress Iman Ouda was rehearsing a scene where she plays a pregnant woman named Haneen. Her character has tried to conceive for nine years, and now she is trapped inside a hospital, giving birth under siege.

In the middle of the scene, an explosion struck nearby, hitting a building and blowing dust into the rehearsal space. The actors covered their mouths and noses and rushed outside. Then, almost as one, they reached for their phones.

“When the place shakes from a nearby bombing, we stop immediately,” Qaddoura says.

“I rush to my phone to call my family, and due to weak network coverage, I live through minutes of true terror.”

Only after they confirmed their families were safe did they return inside to continue rehearsals.

At 25, Ouda has been acting for six years. Calm and expressive in conversation, she sits upright as she speaks, punctuating her words with gentle, focused gestures. War has taught her another skill: distinguishing the sounds above her.

When Apache helicopters or reconnaissance drones drew closer, she says, the actors often kept rehearsing. Their eyes would briefly gaze towards the sky or meet across the room.

“The connection between my real self and the role is fear,” she says. “Would I finish the show and return home, or what would happen? I became a person who fears everything, loss and joy alike.”

Sometimes, it took only a name to bring that fear and loss rushing back.

When Abu Yasin introduced a character called Missing Youssef, Ouda began to cry. Her own father was named Youssef. He had been killed during the war. Later, Israeli forces bulldozed the cemetery where he had been buried; his family could no longer locate his grave.

For Tamer Najm, another actor, the resemblance between life and script came through fatherhood.

Najm, 35, plays Khaled, a man who has spent years trying to have a child with his wife, only to find himself trapped in a hospital during their final IVF attempt.

Before the war, Najm had saved for years to buy an apartment in Gaza City’s Nasser neighbourhood. The apartment was destroyed.

He and his pregnant wife moved between friends’ homes, his in-laws, sidewalks and tents. Their second child was born during the war.

“I was not acting the character of ‘Khaled’; I was living him,” Najm says.

“I had actually been displaced with my pregnant wife from the north amidst fire and danger, terrified every moment that she might lose her baby.”

Every time Najm left for rehearsal, his wife worried about whether he would return. Before leaving, he would tell her: “If you hear a nearby bombing, don’t go outside; take care of yourself and the baby.”

Then he would walk out to play a man afraid of losing his family. “We left with our hands on our hearts, knowing that stepping out in Gaza means returning either safely or in a shroud.”

Yet for Najm, staying home was not necessarily the safer choice emotionally. After losing his home and being repeatedly displaced with his pregnant wife, he saw performing as a way to resist despair and process what he had lived through. Theatre, he felt, allowed him not only to confront but to document his own trauma – and to carry something of Gaza’s experience beyond the places where they were living it.

Eventually, Abu Yasin found them a stage.

The A.M. Qattan Foundation offered its cultural centre on Al-Wehda Street in Gaza City. The centre had been closed and unavailable during the early stages of the project because of the security situation, severe power outages and damage in the surrounding area.

In any case, Abu Yasin says, the project had begun simply as a writing workshop: The company only approached formal cultural venues once the script was complete, the actors had been cast and the work was ready to move onto a stage.

Several of the actors had performed there before the war. After months of tents, asphalt and cramped rooms, they were back inside a theatre.

Just days before opening night on July 19, an Israeli missile struck nearby during rehearsal. The building shook, while scraps of debris fell from the ceiling. Then came the screams from outside.

Five people were killed nearby, Gaza medics reported to local press.

On July 19, they prepared for their first audience.

By 4:30pm, people were filling the roughly 150-seat auditorium. Admission was free.

Behind the curtain, Ouda was trembling. “I was so afraid the electricity would cut out, or that a nearby bombardment would happen and force us to stop the play mid-performance.”

There were no elaborate costumes. They wore everyday clothes gathered from displacement tents and applied what make-up they had in cracked mirrors and by the light of their phones.

Qaddoura stepped onto the stage and became the doctor who could not save his son. Ouda became Haneen, giving birth under siege. Najm became Khaled, trying to protect the family he had waited years to have.

For 50 minutes, the actors performed versions of lives they had carried with them into the theatre.

Among those watching was Najm’s five-year-old daughter, his elder child. His second child, the baby his wife had been carrying during their displacement, had been born during the war.

She cried when she saw her father onstage, covered in dust and dressed in torn clothes. Afterward, she took one of the prop dolls into her arms.

“Dad, I cried when I saw you crying on stage because you looked just like you do at home when you get stressed or worry about us.”

His wife told him: “I didn’t feel like I was watching an actor; I was watching you and our real struggles at home. It felt as though you opened the front door of our house to the entire audience.”

The play went on tour through Gaza in late July through to August, with performances in Daraj, Deir el-Balah, Nuseirat and Khan Younis. At a wedding hall in Khan Younis, the company says more than 500 people attended.

“This performance was a message to the occupation that destroyed all of Gaza’s theatres: Theatre cannot be destroyed,” he says.

“It requires theatre makers, writers and directors, and even if the halls are destroyed, we can perform in the street.”

As the cotton-sheet curtain falls and the stage lights go dark, Qaddoura’s 50 minutes are over.

He gathers his family and begins the journey home. His seven-year-old daughter Sham has fallen asleep, so he carries her.

Outside, the streets are dark. The family uses their mobile phones to light the way as distant shelling sounds across Gaza.

When they reach the rooftop room where they are staying, Qaddoura puts Sham down. The other children are still waiting to eat.

So he returns to the task that began his day. Qaddoura lights a fire. Then he and his wife begin cooking dinner.

articles.title: Melania Trump Faces New Major Backlash Amid Claims Her Marriage With Donald Is ‘Not in a Healthy Place’
articles.summary: "Way to read the room."
articles.body:
Melania Trump faces backlash for sharing a video showcasing preparations for a state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping on X.

X users criticize Melania for being "tone deaf" and "out of touch" with Americans struggling to afford groceries, gas, and healthcare.

Reports suggest Melania and Donald Trump's marriage is strained, with claims that they "barely speak to each other" amid allegations of the POTUS' close relationship with his executive assistant.

Melania Trump is facing major backlash for her latest move.

On Thursday, September 17, the First Lady shared a black-and-white video on X, showcasing preparations for President Donald Trump 's state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The short clip highlights a lavish chandelier and floral centerpieces, and even shows Melania carefully arranging elegant silverware and glassware on the dinner table.

"THE WHITE HOUSE STATE DINNER," she wrote alongside the video. "Every detail considered. An experience thoughtfully conceived and exquisitely realized for our distinguished guests."

As expected, many X users took to the replies and dubbed Melania as "tone deaf" and "out of touch."

"Meanwhile, back on Earth 1, Americans can't afford groceries, gas, or healthcare," one person wrote.

Another X user commented sarcastically, "Way to read the room. You are in touch with the American people. Truly."

"Trumps all have no class so you'll never do right and delete this tweet about your opulent meal BUT did you consider that Americans are choosing between food, medicine, gas & paying to keep power on?" a third user said . "Do you think we give a good godd—n about your dinner plans?

Someone else noted, "Because of your husband's tariffs and interest rates, my family can't afford to renovate our house. But glad y'all had a fancy dinner."

This latest controversy comes amid claims that Melania and Donald Trump's marriage is "not in a healthy place." According to The Irish Star , the POTUS' close relationship with his executive assistant, Natalie Harp , has further strained his connection with Melania. Reportedly, the two barely speak to each other these days.

"A marriage where two people are reportedly barely speaking is clearly not in a healthy place. Communication is the heartbeat of any long term relationship," relationship expert Gemma Logan told the outlet. "When conversation becomes minimal, couples can start living parallel lives rather than a shared one. At that point, the question isn't simply whether they spend time together, but whether they still feel emotionally connected when they do."

Still, Logan remains optimistic that Melania and Trump will overcome the challenges and come back stronger than ever.

"If reports about Donald and Melania Trump are accurate, the most important thing to remember is that distance in a marriage doesn't always mean the relationship is over," she added. "Some couples need constant closeness to feel connected. Others function with far more independence, particularly when both partners have demanding lives, strong personalities and very different ways of dealing with public attention."

Logan explained that many marriages "can survive distance" as long as an "emotional disconnection" doesn't develop between the couple. "Living in different places doesn't automatically spell trouble. Plenty of couples have successful relationships while spending significant periods apart because of work, family responsibilities or lifestyle choices."

"The real issue is what happens emotionally during that time," she emphasized. "If the distance is mutually agreed, openly discussed and balanced with genuine affection, it can work. In some cases, a little breathing room can even make a relationship stronger."

Logan continued, "However, if physical distance is being used to avoid conflict, emotional intimacy or difficult conversations, it can become a sign of a much deeper problem. The key question for Donald and Melania Trump is whether their separate routines are simply practical or whether they reflect a relationship that has become increasingly separate in every meaningful sense."

articles.title: 'Resident Evil' Review: Director Zach Cregger delivers infectious reboot to gory video game franchise
articles.summary: Fox News Digital reviews Sony Pictures' "Resident Evil" starring Austin Abrams, Paul Walter Hauser, Kali Reis and Zach Cherry. Directed by Zach Cregger.
articles.body: Zach Cregger might not be your cup of tea, but his incredible gift behind the camera cannot be ignored. The writer/director comes armed with absolute terror and hilarity, two things that seem incompatible on the surface, yet he's able to blend seamlessly. And his latest horror film, "Resident Evil," is no different. BOX OFFICE COMEBACK: HOW SUMMER 2026 OFFERS A GLIMMER OF HOPE FOR HOLLYWOOD IN THE POST-COVID ERA If "Resident Evil" sounds familiar, that's because it's a long-running video game franchise that turned into a long-running movie franchise starring Milla Jovovich. In this version of "Resident Evil," her character Alice is nowhere to be found. Instead, it stars Austin Abrams, who plays a medical courier named Bryan urgently tasked with delivering what he believes is a vital organ to a hospital in Raccoon City. 'THE DOG STARS' REVIEW: JACOB ELORDI FIGHTS FOR SURVIVAL IN RIDLEY SCOTT'S DULL POST-APOCALYPTIC WESTERN What was supposed to be a quiet, uneventful drive devolves into a series of unfortunate events for Bryan, the cause of which stems from a lab leak of a virus (we all know how easily this can happen, right?) developed by the Umbrella Corporation that transforms organisms into what can only be described as ungodly monsters from the darkest of nightmares. The "Resident Evil" movies we've been used to feature Jovovich being a gun-slinging badass with a zombie body count in the thousands. Here, the scrawny Bryan can barely figure out how to turn the safety off. He's not your knight in shining armor — in fact, he's kind of an idiot. Yet, there's something endearing and relatable about him. It was a bold choice for Cregger to cast Abrams as Bryan. You may recognize Abrams for his stints in "Euphoria" and "This Is Us" or various movies, like Cregger's 2025 Oscar-winning breakout "Weapons," but he hasn't been the star of such a high-profile project, particularly as big as this. His performance is able to generate big laughs as he maintains such seriousness (after all, Bryan is literally fighting for survival). "Resident Evil" should hopefully mark a new chapter in Abrams' career as a leading man — because he's certainly capable. Abrams is essentially a one-man show, but Paul Walter Hauser ("Richard Jewell," "I, Tonya"), Kali Reis ("True Detective") and Zach Cherry ("Severance") make memorable, albeit brief, appearances. ‘MUTINY’ REVIEW: JASON STATHAM TAKES NO PRISONERS IN MINDLESS BUT AMUSING BRAWLER FLICK ON THE HIGH SEAS As a fan of the original source material, Cregger brings the video game experience to life, playing around with first-person angles as we see from Bryan's view of where he's aiming his gun, or the tracking shot as we follow him in the snowy terrain or an eerily quiet house. He and co-writer Shay Hatten (who wrote the more recent "John Wick" installments) were able to stick the landing by juggling bloody thrills with gallows humor. And no offense to Cregger's franchise predecessor Paul W.S. Anderson, but the production value is just far superior in this "Resident Evil" between the cinematography from Oscar nominee Dariusz Wolski ("The Martian"), the score from brothers Hays and Ryan Holladay and the editing from Joe Murphy (all of whom worked on "Weapons" and Cregger's solo feature debut "Barbarian") as well as the gruesome special effects and makeup work. ‘THE END OF OAK STREET’ REVIEW: ANNE HATHAWAY, EWAN MCGREGOR FIGHT DINOSAURS IN SURPRISINGLY FUN MOVIE While it's difficult to rank this higher than "Barbarian" and "Weapons" ("Barbarian" is still my favorite of the three), Cregger is flexing his muscles taking on a Hollywood franchise and has cemented his status among the small elite group of rising filmmakers who have had such a strong streak so early in their careers (think Jordan Peele or Yorgos Lanthimos). And if he keeps it up, perhaps he can reach Christopher Nolan's status where audiences flock to see his movies because the man in the director's chair has become the real star. CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS The Verdict "Resident Evil" comes back to life in this fun, infectious reboot thanks to Zach Cregger's brilliance behind the camera and Austin Abrams' charming performance as an unlikely lead in front of it. If you can't stomach the gore, this isn't for you. But for those who get a kick out of it, get that bucket of popcorn ready. ★★★ ½ — SEE IT NOW "Resident Evil" is rated R for strong bloody violence, gore and language throughout. articles.title: John Ritter's widow Amy Yasbeck details the fatal misdiagnosis she says led to his death
articles.summary: Amy Yasbeck reveals John Ritter was misdiagnosed with a heart attack the night he died, when a CT scan could have detected his aortic dissection.
articles.body: John Ritter's widow Amy Yasbeck is opening up about the actor's final hours more than two decades after his death. In September 2003, Ritter died at the age of 54 after suffering an acute aortic dissection, a tear in the inner layer of the aorta, the body's largest artery that delivers blood away from the heart. Ahead of Aortic Dissection Awareness Week and what would have been Ritter's 78th birthday on Sept. 17, Yasbeck, who founded the John Ritter Foundation for Aortic Health, and the actor's son, Tyler Ritter, who serves on its board, joined Fox News Digital for an interview. CARLY PEARCE SAYS HEART CONDITION LEFT HER FEARING A HEART ATTACK: ‘IS MY HEART OK?’ Looking back on her husband's death, Yasbeck recalled how Ritter was mistakenly treated for a heart attack after arriving at the hospital, which she said "led to what eventually happened." "John was sadly misdiagnosed on the night he passed away," Yasbeck said. "And they didn't do any imaging, but he looked like the guy — right age, right weight, everything — to have a heart attack, and he had chest pain," she continued. "So they just started loading him up with blood thinners and stuff." "And this is sad because it was the opposite. It wasn't a block in his heart, it was a tear in his aorta, so everything they did that night led to what eventually happened," Yasbeck said. "Because there are ways, once it starts dissecting, if you get to the hospital in time, your chances are way better of living." Following Ritter's death, Yasbeck filed a wrongful death lawsuit alleging Ritter's aortic dissection was misdiagnosed. In 2008, a jury found in favor of the two physicians remaining in the case. WATCH: JOHN RITTER'S DEATH HIT SO HARD BECAUSE ‘YOU FELT LIKE YOU KNEW HIM’: FOUNDATION CEO To mark Aortic Dissection Awareness Week, which runs from Sept. 13 to 19, the John Ritter Foundation for Aortic Health, is launching its "50 for 50" campaign, encouraging supporters to donate $50 while drawing attention to the fact that up to 50% of people who suffer an aortic dissection die before reaching medical care. Yasbeck told Fox News Digital that she believes annual estimates of aortic dissections likely undercount the number of cases because patients who die before arriving at a hospital often are not included in the data. She said that improving awareness of the condition is one of the most effective ways to reduce those deaths. However, Yasbeck emphasized that raising awareness is not just for patients and families. She pointed out the importance of ensuring doctors recognize that chest pain can signal an aortic dissection, not just a heart attack. COUNTRY STAR ASHLEY COOKE SPEAKS OUT ABOUT RARE HEART CONDITION THAT COULD END HER LIFE AT ANY MOMENT "Your heart can be in perfect shape," she said. "You can be an athlete." "And if the blood that's being pumped into your aorta is going inside the layers of the aorta, instead of being traveled to all of the rest of the highway where it's supposed to go, it's curtains for you," she continued. "So it's so important to be able to have that awareness," Yasbeck added. "And there's no drug for aortic dissection at this point in time. For blood pressure, which sometimes can help you if you are at risk, right? Keep your blood pressure down, but there's no instant fix for it. You have to be a participant in your own health in this regard. And by doing that, you are also protecting your family. For generations, actually." Yasbeck said she recently witnessed firsthand how her husband's story has become part of emergency medicine. She recalled accompanying a friend with chest pain to the hospital where medical staff told her they were ordering a CT scan to check for "the John Ritter thing" to rule out an aortic dissection. "They said, 'We're checking for the John Ritter thing', not knowing who I am, not knowing whom my friend is that was a friend of John's," she remembered. "It was just like this relief came over me. And my buddy, you know, gave me the thumbs up." "The fact that they said checking for that ‘John Ritter thing,’ talking shorthand to me, I freaking love that. Call it whatever you want. CT scan, a CAT scan, is the gold standard for diagnosing in an emergency situation, in any situation, but to be able to realize as soon as you can, ‘This is not a heart attack. This is an aortic dissection,’" she continued. "'Fix this a whole different way.'" 'GAME OF THRONES' STAR EMILIA CLARKE WAS CONVINCED SHE 'CHEATED DEATH' AFTER SURVIVING TWO BRAIN ANEURYSMS While speaking with Fox News Digital, Yasbeck shared that doctors and researchers had told her for years that Ritter's death marked a turning point in awareness of aortic dissection. "There was kind of a pre-John Ritter awareness of aortic dissection and a post," she said. "Sadly, John died in the last hours of pre-John Ritter awareness." WATCH: JOHN RITTER'S LEGACY IS HELPING PREVENT DEADY AORTIC DISSECTIONS, DOCTOR SAYS Since Ritter's death, the "Three's Company" star's family has worked through the John Ritter Foundation for Aortic Health to raise awareness about thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections. A thoracic aortic aneurysm is an enlargement of the body's main artery that can often be detected through screening before it tears into an aortic dissection, a life-threatening emergency. Ritter's widow and his children have encouraged people to learn about their family medical history and seek appropriate screening when they are at increased risk because thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections can have a genetic component. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Yasbeck said doctors now believe Ritter's father likely died from an undiagnosed aortic dissection, while routine screenings after his death revealed the same condition in his brother Tom, allowing him to undergo life-saving surgery before it became fatal. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE Tyler, 41, told Fox News Digital that becoming aware of his family history in the aftermath of his father's death had changed his approach to his own health. Ritter shared Tyler as well as son Jason Ritter, 46, and daughter Carly Ritter, 44, with his first wife, actress Nancy Morgan. Yasbeck, who was Ritter's second wife, shared son Noah Ritter, 28. "It's impossible not to imagine that there's a parallel universe where the family demanded an autopsy on our grandfather and discovered an aortic dissection, which led to my dad and his brother getting screened," Tyler said. "And as we see with Tommy, as Amy just said, Tommy is still alive and doing great." "It's just too easy to imagine that in this other universe, where my grandfather was properly diagnosed, that my dad would be totally fine right now with just an aortic replacement surgery," he continued. "And that, on the one hand, is very difficult to accept and to comprehend." GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "On the other hand, it has provided a massive silver lining," Tyler added. "I get scanned every year. My kids know I get scanned. They know why I get scanned. They know that my dad was the last one in our family. Our mission is that he is the last in our family to suffer a dissection." Tyler said watching his own children discover their grandfather through episodes of "Three's Company" has reinforced the importance of preserving Ritter's legacy through awareness. He explained that though aneurysms are often asymptomatic, they can be detected through screening, which is why he encourages families with a history of aortic disease or unexplained early deaths to speak with their doctors. WATCH: JOHN RITTER FOUNDATION CEO RECALLS SURVIVING LIFE-THREATENING AORTIC DISSECTION "The more you know," he said. "If you can spot in a first-degree relative that there's a potential for a missed or undiagnosed illness or disease, it would just be worth asking your doctor." Looking back, Tyler said his father's death remains a tragedy, but one that has helped protect other families. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It is unfortunate. It's a tragedy," he said. articles.title: Anamanaguchi has ‘too goddamn many’ browser tabs open right now
articles.summary: The chiptune rock band known for Scott Pilgrim game soundtracks and a Hatsune Miku collab answered our weekly questionnaire to celebrate their new single, “Yeah I Guess.”
articles.body: Anamanaguchi, the band consisting of Peter Berkman, James DeVito, Luke Silas, and Ary Warnaar, are most known for their chiptune music. Like me, you might have first heard them in game soundtracks like 2010’s Scott Pilgrim vs. the World: The Game or know of their collaboration with Hatsune Miku (which even made its way into Fortnite). They’ve gone through different eras of breakneck chiptune beats and dance-y pop songs, but their 2025 album Anyway took an indie rock departure — recorded in person at the American Football house and filled with fuzzy guitars. They’re also a band that’s terminally online and very plugged into the video game scene as well as the weirder sides of the internet — just listen to Peter and Luke’s guest spot on the Panic World podcast talking about Etsy witches. Anamanaguchi has a new single, “Yeah I Guess,” continuing in the musical direction of Anyway. And if it’s a precursor to a new album dropping soon, I’m sure I’ll be looping it endlessly just as I did the tracks “Magnet,” “Fall Away,” and “Valley of Silence.” (Seriously, I’ve at times had Anyway set on repeat for hours straight.) Not only did all four members of Anamanaguchi agree to answer our weekly questionnaire, but they answered all our questions. [Media: What is your most indispensable tool? Luke Silas: I think my most used tool is Ableton Live Operator, it is simple and powerful and can make basic things happen incredibly quickly. I usually open it up just for writing or getting ideas down, but more often than not the sounds I get with it tend to make it to the final product! Which is the most underappreciated? Ary Warnaar: Built-in laptop mic and cellphone mic aren’t exactly slept on, but def underappreciated. They’re great for just getting ideas down fast, but now they sound so good that I find myself not even re-recording what I thought would be “scratch” vocals. Peter Berkman: Right now it’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S. Best mouse I’ve ever had. It has a sideways scroll. It has a button to switch between notched and smooth scroll wheel. The click is satisfying but still really quiet. It’s really sensitive & responsive on whatever surface I happen to have it on. It feels really good in my hand. It charges directly into a USB-C port without external batteries so it gets to look like a mouse with a tail after it’s worked really hard. When I’m at a different computer, or if I’m on a laptop having to use a trackpad, I feel like I’ve lost so much gestural fidelity. I love the keyboard but let’s be real Douglas Engelbart cooked when he invented the mouse. But he didn’t have the recipe of the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and he didn’t even live to see it. The LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S wasn’t even invented until June 2022. I have seen two friends recently using the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and I say “Hey man that’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S” I use that thing too. James DeVito: Lately it’s been an app called “Amphetamine” that keeps your computer from going to sleep for a set amount of time. It’s great when starting an export/render or other task that may take a while and then being able to throw my laptop in my bag and have it work while I head elsewhere… Just gotta make sure the laptop doesn’t ’splode in your bag from overheating. LS: I love metronomes! Strengthening time is so important, and getting more comfortable with a metronome means you get to play around with time more confidently! I would love people to love metronomes the way I do! What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer? LS: Probably Discord? Let’s say Discord. What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone? AW: Would kill to get a normal 1/8-inch headphone out again. I’ve been constantly replacing dongles ever since Apple ditched the headphone out. Because they break or or get misplaced. Frustrating and wasteful. JD: A wise friend of mine once taught me to increase the key-repeat on my computer beyond what is normally allowed via the UI. It feels insane at first but your hand/brain coordination catches up with the speed eventually and then you can tttttttttttttttype and deleeeeeeete things so much quicker. LS: The only thing I’d like to add to my iPhone SE is a USB port so I can type with a keyboard because I suck at typing on my phone. What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar? LS: I have never done this before! I probably should!! PB: There’s a new radio aggregator called vvorldwide.com. It’s amazing. It’s like having a radio dial in your car except it pools the feeds from NTS, The Lot, dublab, KEXP, loads of different places from all over the world. It’s one of those products that’s like: Wow. Why did nobody think to make this before? It’s so useful, lightweight, and beautiful. It’s amazing to me how detached from reality and human use the big companies are (and have been for a long time). It’s one of those refreshing things you see, it reminds me of The Unfinished Revolution by Michael Dertouzos. You can just build things you want to see! JD: Gmail :( How many tabs do you have open right now? PB: Tab grouping from Firefox has become an artform for me. I don’t see tabs anymore just folders of memory I can recall like a PSX save file. LS: 46 and 31 between two windows. Too goddamn many. Most of them are meant to be shared with others or read/watched, every weekend I do a cleanout but there are truthfully a few that have been sitting for months. I can’t be the only one. JD: I like when Chrome on my phone stops displaying the number of open tabs and just shows a smiley face :) Which social media platform do you use the most? LS: Staying detached from social media tends to be better for my mental health on the day-to-day, but scrolling following on Twitter is the easiest way for me to stay connected to games or news still. Instagram stresses me out lately more than ever before. YouTube definitely counts and I do love it very much, but shorts are a rare treat; I tend to watch long-form stuff mostly or have different content with no dialogue on a second monitor, like either a video game longplay or lots of restoration or cooking videos. What is your happy place online? AW: Facebook marketplace. Specifically low-balling “I know what I got” type mfs. No one ever accepts my offers, but I think it’s important to keep people humble, and long term, I’d like to think that I’m contributing to keeping the prices low for the next buyers. PB: I’ve just discovered clothes. So I’m hunting a lot on places like Grailed or Depop or whatever. It’s a lot like the way I treat musical equipment on Reverb. It’s fun to sell stuff and buy stuff… when it’s equal amounts it feels more like barter and temporary sharing. LS: Video game speedruns! Twitch streams like GDQ or RPG Limit Break are very comforting to me and a very sweet community of fun personalities. What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned? JD: 3D printers. I’ve been 3D printing for a long time now, and it’s gotten so so so much more reliable/easy at this point. The fact that I can design a bracket etc. for stage production and have it in hand within an hour really is the future. LS: I’m going to say my Game Boy counts for this question. I use it less for sound design than I used to, but I bought new flash cartridges recently for the first time in years, and I’m ready to get cooking with it again very soon! It’s a perfect little self-contained workstation. Which was the most disappointing? LS: I’ve bought a few different effects plugins that tend to have some distinct effects but end up not giving me what I’m looking for, or feel far too specific to a use case for me to reach for generally speaking. I’ve found more exciting results from stacking and tweaking stock effects than I have reaching for dedicated single-use stuff. PB: I’m not gonna hate on here… but they exist. What game do you have the fondest memories of? PB: Return of the Obra Dinn was so much fun. Any game that feels like detective work is the kinda thing that gets me going, and instantly creates a moment of excitement for me that stays frozen that I can always go back to. I think about playing [the original] Resident Evil for the first time, the first three Phoenix Wright games: I can tell you everything about where I was and what I was feeling when I first played those games. It’s not even a nostalgia based thing. I played Parasite Eve II for the first time two years ago and it was an instant deep love. LS: I think my favorite video game of all time is Chrono Trigger. It was a world I really wished I could experience in real life and the atmosphere of every place you go is special to me. I have been trying to rip off Yasunori Mitsuda and Nobuo Uematsu every time I write for the last 30 years. It’s the first game I think of when I want to start a new playthrough of something familiar to me! Which tech trend do you wish would go away? AW: I don’t like forced two step authentication or even worse, the upper case + number + symbol extra long type passwords. Like if I want my password to just be the letter “a,” that’s on me. I’m comfortable with that choice. I’m comfortable with that level of vulnerability. Shit maybe I don’t even want a password sometimes. Just leave it all out there for the people. LS: Using AI to make music! Blue check accounts on twitter talking about using AI to make music! Write your own fucking music, have fun learning a skill that will continue to give and build and bloom until the day you die!!! What is one thing you wish you had created? LS: “Show Me Love” by Robin S. is a perfect song, and every time I hear it I think “God, I wish that could have been mine.” The combination of the M1 organ, that 909 groove, and Robin S.’ top line is like a simple meal where the right ingredients add up to something far greater than the sum of their parts; a perfect BLT, a chocolate/vanilla/peanut butter milkshake, the freshest sushi you’ve ever eaten. JD: The Black Eyed Peas performed at the 2020 VMAs and they all had light up crotches that sync’d up to the show. Why the f didn’t they call me to do that? What creation are you most proud of? PB: Going back and listening to our album Anyway always surprises me. I love it so much. I think it’s the kinda thing that people who didn’t get it will eventually come around on. Sleeper classic even for me ha. LS: I think the song “Really Like To” from our latest album Anyway is a song that accomplishes a lot of the things I want to when writing for the band! It’s loud and fast, has fun drum parts, fun to sing along to, and I got to do an ambient section at the end; I like showing it to people as an indication of where we’re at right now. JD: Anyway as well — the entire process was so collaborative throughout. A lot of really great memories writing at the house and recording at Tarbox Road Studios. Which are you least proud of? LS: In 2023 I tried to get good at baking cookies, and in the process made a batch of not only the worst cookies I’ve ever had, but some of the worst food I have ever experienced. They looked great, but on a first bite tasted like absolutely nothing and had a texture of chewing damp sand, and on a second bite a bitter taste began to crawl across my tongue that practically gagged me. The only other human who tasted them was my next-door neighbor, just so I could have a witness to the crime that I’d committed. To this day I’m still not sure how I fucked up that bad, and I’ll never forget that taste. What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received? AW: When I was a kid I met Steve Lukather, the guitarist of Toto, and I told him I wanted to be a guitarist in a band when I grow up. He told me that if I wanted to get the girls I had to either lift weights or get good at guitar solos. I’ve done neither and I’ve been suspicious of all advice ever since. PB: My dad told me to “never give up” when I was playing Zelda in my basement as a kid. It gave me a big affinity for puzzles, very encouraging. My dad still gives me important advice at all the big moments in my life — I am very grateful to have him. LS: Progress, not perfection. What is your current obsession? PB: Investigating criminal networks of the 1990s! More of a hobby than an obsession. LS: I’ve unfortunately found myself going further down the rabbit hole of Deltarune theory videos. I don’t buy into the majority of the speculation shared, but I love the game and there is lots of incredible insight shared into the design of it and aspects of it mechanically and narratively that I didn’t even realize I was missing. What do you do when you need to focus? AW: Modafinil. Jk lol, I try not to force focusing and just let it be a byproduct of inspiration/motivation. I wait for the focus to come. If I’m having trouble focusing on something then I probably shouldn’t be doing it. Like driving a car. And if you attach rituals to focus it just invites the possibility of not being able to focus without said rituals. LS: I wait until about 8pm, charge my phone on the other side of my studio, get a large cup of black coffee, put on my second monitor a very long playthrough of a game I’m already familiar with (most recent one was Grandia II), and keep my door shut as long as possible. What do you do when you’re feeling stuck? LS: Take a walk down the Venice boardwalk, get a two-dollar salad from Chairman Mao’s, and eat while listening to music and watching people skate at the Venice bowl. PB: It’s very important to fuck off for a minute. I will go out to a Smash tournament in the Dallas area. There’s a very lively scene that’s super competitive and full of great people. I can always go back from that feeling fresh. When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone? PB: My phone’s dead half the time so it’s a moment that can happen anytime. LS: I legitimately don’t remember and that depresses me!! I don’t like that!! What’s the last piece of physical media you bought? LS: About a month ago I picked up a used copy of Only Theatre of Pain by Christian Death at Headline Records, great shop I’ve been going to since I was a kid! JD: I recently bought a record of a band called “Schlong” at Permanent Records in LA. I love finding stuff that isn’t available on streaming. It can be really easy to get complacent with what’s available online but there’s so much out there in the real world!!! What do you think is worth splurging on? LS: I think the most consistent answer for me is special meals. Something unique in another country, or something really special to which I don’t get to treat myself often. It’s always food! AW: Vacation/travel/time off/adventure etc... I wish it wasn’t considered so much of a splurge. The same way you wouldn’t really call going on a hike a splurge, but in a world where just existing can be expensive, I think it’s something that’s tremendously good for the ~soul~, and worth regularly “splurging” some time/money on. I want to talk to my friends about what cool missions they went on this summer, not what new shoes they bought or whatever. PB: Gonna agree 100% with Ary. The value of travel can’t be overemphasized. What would the tagline for your biopic be? AW: “If you cant handle him at his fastest, you don’t deserve him at his furiousest” JD: “Better to waste than to have not” PB: “You know he had to do it to em” LS: “Life is Hectic.” What’s the last GIF or meme you used? articles.title: History-making Miss USA reveals how she got swimsuit-ready while raising 2 young kids
articles.summary: Justus Kelley reveals how she prepped for the Miss USA pageant during nap times and bath routines while caring for her two young foster children.
articles.body: Justus Kelley made history as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss USA — and she got there in an unconventional way. On Aug. 27, the organization hosted the 75th edition of the national pageant in Miami. The 31-year-old, who was Miss Virginia USA 2026, succeeded last year’s winner, Audrey Eckert, 24. The pageant opened the competition to married women and mothers in 2023. "My pageant prep, it did look different," Kelley told Fox News Digital. "I'm not going to pretend like I was able to dedicate the same amount of time as what I did in the past. I had to get creative. Their nap time was my prep time. It was late nights. It was after the bath and bed routine. I did walking classes with my baby on my chest, in his carrier. I did squats in my living room while holding my two-year-old. I practiced interview questions while feeding my toddler." NAVY VETERAN TRADES MILITARY UNIFORM FOR MISS GEORGIA SASH FOLLOWING HEARTBREAKING LOSS "There were days when I wished I could just take the entire day to dedicate to pageant prep, but that's not where I am," Kelley said. "That's not the season of life that I'm in. And we made it work, and my family was fully on board with this experience. They know that they're along for the journey; they're along for this ride with me." The Miss USA pageant began in 1952 in Long Beach, California, with New York's Jackie Loughery becoming its first winner. The competition is separate from the Miss America pageant, which traces its history to a 1921 event in Atlantic City, New Jersey. Kelley, a foster mom of two, is the first married mother to retain the Miss USA title. In 1957, Mary Leona Gage was crowned Miss USA but was stripped of the title the following day after pageant organizers learned she was married and the mother of two sons. WATCH: MISS USA 2026 REVEALS HOW SHE TRAINED FOR PAGEANT WITH KIDS IN TOW Kelley said she ditched social media and TV in favor of workouts whenever she found a spare moment while caring for her two young children. "I love abductor and adductor exercises, something that I usually do on a machine at the gym," she explained. "But if I can't make it to the gym, I'm just lying on the floor, elevating my leg and mirroring what I would've done on that machine. For me, leading up to a pageant, knowing there's a fitness component, I'm going to be in a swimsuit on that stage. I want to feel good. I want to show off all this hard work." "I really focused on core," she said. "So a lot of times you'll find me at home in the living room. I might be watching a movie or doing some self-care, but I am on the floor crunching it out during that movie, saying, 'Let's try to get through this whole scene doing crunches,' and then you pause. It was really all about focusing on core." Kelley said her husband's support also helped her through the competition. "The crown might be his because all he keeps saying is, 'I can't believe I'm Mr. USA,'" Kelley said with a laugh, referring to her college sweetheart. "I'm like, 'Babe, I don't know if that might be trademarked. Stop saying that!'" "He is so over the moon," Kelley said. "We've been together for 13, going on 14 years and married for nine. He's been a part of every bit of this journey. I've been competing for over 10 years now. And from my very first pageant, he was there holding a sign with my face on it up until the very end. I did not get here alone. He's been a huge supporter. My husband's a consultant, and he's been calling himself my pageant consultant. But he's been a huge help in getting me to this point." "The prize that made me go, 'Wow, and I have some questions,' was knowing that the Range Rover is a part of traveling in style even after your year as Miss USA. I think that's huge. But my first question was, 'Does it fit car seats?'" Kelley said she wants her year as Miss USA to challenge the idea that women need to choose between their families, careers and personal dreams. "You don't have to choose one part of who you are," Kelley said. "You can be all of who you are. That, to me, is the message. We can embrace every part of who we are. It doesn't take away from the other. It doesn't mean there aren't trade-offs, and there aren't times when we have to lean on our village more heavily to get through all the things that we may be pursuing. But know that we don't have to sacrifice ourselves." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? articles.title: Carrot Top hospitalized, forced to cancel weekend performances
articles.summary: Carrot Top was hospitalized in Las Vegas, forcing cancellations of his residency shows. His rep says the comedian is recovering and asks for privacy.
articles.body: Carrot Top has been hospitalized in Las Vegas, Fox News Digital can confirm. The comedian, whose real name is Scott Thompson, has a standing show at Luxor Las Vegas Hotel and Casino. His regular shows on Friday and Saturday have been canceled. "Mr. Thompson is recovering in the hospital and is receiving the care and support he needs," Thompson's representative told Fox News Digital. "His family and those closest to him are deeply grateful for the concern, prayers and respectfully ask for privacy." BARRY MANILOW, 82, GIVES UPDATE ON HIS CANCER BATTLE AS HE CANCELS MORE TOUR DATES When reached by the Las Vegas Review-Journal, a spokesperson for MGM Resorts said, "Scott is a beloved member of the Luxor and MGM Resorts family, and we are relieved to hear that he is recovering. We are thinking of him and wish him strength as he receives the care and support he needs." The outlet also reported that Thompson was seen at a bar in town around 2 p.m. on Friday, hours before his show was set to begin at 8 p.m. As of now, tickets for his shows next week are still available for purchase. articles.title: Snooki announces ‘mawma is cancer free’ after diagnosis, hysterectomy
articles.summary: Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi shared the good news in a video that featured the reality star sipping a celebratory drink.
articles.body: Congratulations are in order! Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi announced in a Sept. 19 Instagram video that she is officially cancer-free. The good news comes after the “Jersey Shore” star told fans in February that she was diagnosed with Stage 1 cervical cancer, undergoing a hysterectomy months later to treat the disease. “After a colposcopy, conization & hysterectomy, mawma is cancer free,” Polizzi, 38, wrote in some text that accompanied a video of the reality star, enjoying a celebratory drink. A colposcopy is a procedure that checks the cervix, vagina and vulva for signs of disease while conization refers to a different procedure in which abnormal tissue is removed from the cervix. The announcement received an outpouring of support, including positive messages from fellow “Jersey Shore” cast mates Mike “The Situation” Sorrentino and Sammi “Sweetheart” Giancola. Other social media users, who have also gone through cervical cancer, shared their excitement for Polizzi. “I’m so happy for you and your family 🥹♥️ I know the struggle you have been through 🥹♥️I got diagnosed with cervix cancer in 2022 and went through chemo and radiation therapy, I’m cancer free now ♥️LOVE from Denmark ♥️” one user wrote. In her post, Polizzi showed her appreciation for her medical team. “Thanks to all the doctors who helped me on this journey!” Polizzi wrote in the caption. “It wouldn’t be possible without you!” The reality star — who shared that she will be getting pap smears every three months to ensure that the disease doesn’t reappear — also encouraged women to be vigilant about their health. “GET UR PAP SMEARS LADIES! & stay on top of those appointments!💗” Polizzi wrote. Back in July, the mother of three shared a video on social media that gave fans a glimpse of her experience with hysterectomy surgery, documenting the entire day of the procedure. “It’s a scary thing, and a lot of us women deal with it, and no one really talks about it,” Polizzi said in the video. “So I’m here to give that platform for all of us ladies.” Polizzi also shared her honest emotions around the surgery. She said in the video that she was “terrified” while going into the procedure. The doctors ended up removing her uterus, cervix along with “some parts” of the vagina “just to make sure we get everything,” she said. “Just dealing with all that pain — it’s not great,” a tearful Polizzi said.
